title: Guru Gobind Singh: sword and saint
hook: the tenth Guru's light: the Khalsa, the song, the courage
tomorrow: after ten Gurus, who is the Guru now?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Tegh Bahadur: freedom for others, a thread he didn't wear, defended anyway. His son, still a boy then, became the tenth Guru.
screen: `FREEDOM FOR OTHERS.` → `HIS SON, THE TENTH GURU.`

segments.voice: Simran started her morning with the Ardas, standing in the kitchen, her own small asks folded inside it. Then she went to the dispatch desk and saw it again: the newest driver, whose English is still shaky, gets the worst routes every week, the long hauls and the late loads. Nobody says anything. She prayed first. Then what does she do? She asks her dad for five minutes, and she brings the route sheets.
screen: `THE ARDAS, IN THE KITCHEN.` → `THE WORST ROUTES, EVERY WEEK.` → `SHE BRINGS THE ROUTE SHEETS.`

segments.voice: Pray, then act bravely: that's the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, in one line. Tradition says that on Vaisakhi at Anandpur he called for volunteers ready to give their heads, and from the Five Beloved who stood up, the Khalsa began: saint-soldiers, sant sipahi, the prayer and the courage in one body. He was a poet too, and his verse is full of this pairing. In Chandi Charitra, in paraphrase: grant me this, that I never turn back from doing good, and never fear the enemy when I go to face it. And in the Zafarnama, his letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, he sets the order: when every other way has failed, it is right to take up the sword. The sword comes last, after words, after patience. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Guru who founded the Khalsa wrote that the sword comes last. For Simran, the sword is a stack of route sheets and a steady voice. Harjit listens, frowns at the sheets, and says: not your business. Simran doesn't argue. She leaves the sheets on his desk.
screen: `PRAY, THEN ACT BRAVELY.` · `THE KHALSA: SAINT-SOLDIERS.` · `NEVER TURN BACK FROM GOOD.` · `THE SWORD COMES LAST.` · then, large: `SWORD AND SAINT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one wrong near you that people keep walking past: at school, at work, at home. Name what's in the way of saying something: fear, awkwardness, not knowing how. Then plan the first brave step, the calm words first, and say the opening sentence quietly to yourself.
Guru Gobind Singh: the tenth Guru, saint and soldier. He made the Khalsa, wrote the song, and put the sword last.
Words for today: sword and saint, the prayer first and then the brave act. Words before anything sharper.

howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate the birth of the Khalsa at Vaisakhi and Guru Gobind Singh's birth at his gurpurab; initiated Sikhs of the Khalsa wear the five Ks, and his compositions such as the Jaap are part of the daily prayers.

fork.setup: a friend says a younger kid is being shaken down for lunch money behind the gym. you pray about it. what's the sword-and-saint next step?
options: keep praying; the saint's part is enough if your heart is right.
go confront the older kids yourself; the sword is for the helpless.
tell an adult you trust what you heard; words before anything sharper.
fork.reveal: pray, then act bravely, in order: words first. the Zafarnama keeps the sword for when every other way has failed.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sant sipahi, saint-soldier; the ideal of the Khalsa.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warrior Guru, mostly about battles.
what it means: a saint-soldier: pray first, act bravely, and keep the sword for last.
what a scholar hears: Chandi Charitra's 'deh shiva bar mohe ihai' asks never to turn back from good; the Zafarnama puts the sword after all other means.

chat.says: talked to dad about the new driver's routes. he said 'not your business.' push it or drop it?
options: push, calmly: bring the route sheets again and ask him to look with you.
drop it; sword and saint means praying for the driver quietly instead.
push hard: go over dad's head and confront the dispatcher yourself.
chat.meaning: Guru Gobind Singh: pray, then act bravely, with words first and the sword last. Calm, steady persistence is the brave step here.

Khalsa.meaning: the community of initiated Sikhs, begun by Guru Gobind Singh

Vaisakhi.meaning: the spring harvest festival, the Khalsa's birthday

Zafarnama.meaning: Guru Gobind Singh's letter in Persian verse to Aurangzeb

Chandi Charitra.meaning: a poem in the Dasam Granth, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh

sources.ref: Chandi Charitra (Dasam Granth), 'deh shiva bar mohe ihai, subh karman te kabhoon na taron...', paraphrased
Zafarnama, verse 22 (when all other means have failed, it is right to take up the sword), paraphrased
Sikh tradition: the founding of the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi; the Five Beloved
